grammar.focus: Have got (reconocimiento): has got; adjetivo + hair
grammar.explanation: En esta misión reconocemos «has got» en descripciones de otras personas. «She has got…» significa «ella tiene…» y «He has got…» significa «él tiene…». Para describir el pelo, el color o la forma aparece antes de «hair»: «curly hair», «straight hair», «brown hair».
grammar.practice: Lee la descripción y elige el personaje con ese pelo.

items.prompt: Choose the correct phrase for one girl.
items.es: Con she, el modelo es has got.
La forma del modelo con he es has got.
El adjetivo curly va antes de hair.
Brown describe el color del pelo.

source.readingText: Look at the three faces. Mia has got curly brown hair and brown eyes. Tom has got straight black hair. His eyes are dark. Ava has got straight blonde hair and a small nose. They have different faces and hair. Can you match each description to the right person?

readingQuestions.question: How many faces are in the text?
Who has got curly brown hair?
Who has got straight black hair?
Is Ava's hair curly or straight?
What is small on Ava's face?
Do the three people have the same hair?
What must the reader do?
readingQuestions.answer: Match each description to a person
options: Match each description to a person

source.listeningScript: Interviewer: Hello, Mia. Tell us about your friends. Mia: Tom has got straight black hair. Interviewer: What about Ava? Mia: Ava has got straight blonde hair. Interviewer: And you, Mia? Mia: I have got curly brown hair. Interviewer: Have you all got the same hair? Mia: No, we have got different hair. Interviewer: Thank you, Mia.

listeningQuestions.question: Who has got straight black hair?
Who has got straight blonde hair?
What kind of hair has Mia got?
Have the three friends got the same hair?

grammar.explanation: Usamos «Put on…» para indicar que alguien se ponga una prenda y «Take off…» para pedir que se la quite. En una instrucción el verbo va al principio: «Put on your coat».
grammar.model: Put on your coat. Take off your shoes.
grammar.practice: Ordena las instrucciones para vestirse según la situación.

items.prompt: It is cold. Choose the instruction.
items.es: Put on significa ponerse.

items.prompt: Your shoes are dirty. Choose the instruction to remove them.
items.es: Take off significa quitarse.
El imperativo usa el verbo base Put.
La instrucción comienza con Take off.

source.readingText: It is a cold morning. Ben is ready for school. First, he puts on his shoes. Then he puts on his coat. He wears a warm hat, too. At home, his sister takes off her coat and shoes. Mum says, “Put on your hat, Ben!” Ben smiles and goes out.

readingQuestions.question: What does Ben put on first?
What does Ben put on after his shoes?
What does Ben wear on his head?
Who takes off her coat and shoes?
What does Mum tell Ben to put on?
What does Ben do at the end?

source.listeningScript: It is a cold day. Anna is at home. She puts on her shoes. Then she puts on her coat. She takes a hat from the chair and puts it on. Her brother is warm. He takes off his coat inside the house. Anna says, “Put on your shoes. It is time to go!” They leave the house together.

listeningQuestions.question: What does Anna put on first?
What does Anna put on next?
Where does Anna take the hat from?
Who takes off a coat inside the house?
What does Anna tell her brother to put on?

grammar.explanation: Un imperativo es una instrucción. Empezamos con el verbo en su forma básica: «Wash your hands», «Brush your teeth» o «Clean the table». No añadimos -s al verbo cuando damos una orden.
grammar.model: Wash your hands. Brush your teeth.
grammar.practice: Ordena las instrucciones de higiene y limpieza en una secuencia lógica.

items.es: El imperativo usa wash, sin -s.
Empezamos la instrucción con Brush.
Clean es el verbo limpiar.

items.prompt: Choose the correct instruction for a dirty table.
items.es: Usamos Clean + objeto para dar la instrucción.

source.readingText: It is cleaning day at home. First, Mia washes her hands with soap. Then she uses a towel. Dad says, “Brush your teeth, please.” Ben cleans the table because it is dirty. After that, the children tidy their toys. The room is clean and tidy now.

readingQuestions.question: What day is it at home?
What does Mia use to wash her hands?
What does Mia use after washing her hands?
Why does Ben clean the table?
What is the room like at the end?
Which word describes the table before Ben cleans it?

source.listeningScript: Mum: It is time to clean the bathroom. Ben: What can I do? Mum: Wash your hands with soap. Ben: OK. Mum: Now brush your teeth. Ben: Where is my towel? Mum: It is next to the sink. Ben: Thank you. Mum: Please tidy your things. The bathroom is clean now.

listeningQuestions.question: What is it time to do?
What does Mum tell Ben to use?
How is the bathroom at the end?

grammar.focus: Imperativos y secuencia sencilla de rutina
grammar.explanation: Para dar instrucciones de higiene usamos el verbo al principio: «Brush your teeth» y «Wash your hands». Podemos ordenar varias acciones con «First» (primero) y «Then» (después).
grammar.model: Brush your teeth. Wash your hands.
grammar.practice: Relaciona cada objeto del baño con la instrucción correspondiente y ordena los pasos.

items.prompt: Which object do you use with toothpaste?
items.es: El cepillo de dientes se usa con pasta de dientes.
La expresión del currículo es Wash your hands.
El imperativo usa el verbo base brush.
Shampoo significa champú.

source.readingText: It is bath time for Ella. First, she takes a shower. She uses shampoo to wash her hair. Then she gets her toothbrush and toothpaste. She brushes her teeth. After that, she washes her hands. Her bath time is finished and she is ready for bed.

source.listeningScript: Presenter: Welcome to Bath Time. Here is a simple routine. First, take a shower. Use shampoo. Then get your toothbrush and toothpaste. Brush your teeth. Next, wash your hands. You can take a bath, too. A shower or a bath helps you get clean. Thank you for listening!

grammar.focus: Presente simple en bloques de acción: I…
grammar.explanation: Para hablar de la rutina usamos «I» + un verbo en presente. Por ejemplo: «I wake up», «I eat» y «I sleep». En esta misión aprendemos estas expresiones como bloques completos, sin añadir terminaciones.
grammar.model: I wake up. I eat. I sleep.
grammar.practice: Ordena tres acciones y completa cada frase con el verbo correcto.

items.prompt: Complete: I ___ up in the morning.
items.es: Con I usamos wake, sin -s.
El modelo de la misión es I + eat.
Sleep significa dormir.
Con I usamos go.

source.readingText: Tom has a busy day. He wakes up in the morning. He gets up and eats breakfast. Then he goes to school. In the afternoon, he plays with his friends. At night, Tom sleeps. He likes his daily routine because every day has time to learn and play.

readingQuestions.question: What does Tom do after he wakes up?
Where does Tom go after breakfast?
When does Tom play with his friends?
What does Tom do at night?

source.listeningScript: Interviewer: Hello, Lily. Tell us about your day. Lily: I wake up in the morning. Interviewer: What do you do next? Lily: I get up and eat breakfast. Interviewer: Do you go to school? Lily: Yes, I go to school. Then I play with my friends. Interviewer: What do you do at night? Lily: I sleep. Interviewer: Thank you, Lily!

listeningQuestions.question: What does she do after waking up?

grammar.focus: What time is it? It is… o’clock
grammar.explanation: Preguntamos la hora con «What time is it?». Para una hora en punto respondemos «It is… o’clock» o «It’s… o’clock». El número va antes de o’clock. En esta misión practicamos horas en punto del uno al doce.
grammar.model: What time is it? It’s one o’clock. It’s twelve o’clock.
grammar.practice: Mira el reloj y completa la respuesta con el número correcto.

items.es: What time is it? pregunta qué hora es.
Para las horas en punto usamos o'clock.

items.prompt: The clock shows 7:00. Choose the answer.
items.es: A las 7:00 decimos seven o'clock.

items.prompt: The clock shows 12:00. Choose the answer.
items.es: A las 12:00 decimos twelve o'clock.

source.readingText: It is Monday. At seven o'clock, Sam wakes up in the morning. At eight o'clock, he eats breakfast. At twelve o'clock, it is lunchtime. In the afternoon, he plays at three o'clock. At six o'clock, it is evening. At nine o'clock, it is night and Sam goes to bed.

readingQuestions.question: What time does Sam wake up?
What moment of the day is it at six o'clock?
What time does Sam go to bed?
What moment of the day is it at seven o'clock in the morning?
How many different clock times are in the text?
What does Sam do at night?

source.listeningScript: Listen to Ben's day. At seven o'clock in the morning, Ben gets up. At eight o'clock, he eats breakfast. At one o'clock in the afternoon, he reads a book. At five o'clock, he plays football. At seven o'clock in the evening, he has dinner. At ten o'clock at night, Ben sleeps.

listeningQuestions.question: Whose day do we hear about?
What time does Ben get up?
What does Ben do at one o'clock?
What does Ben do at five o'clock?
Which moment of the day is one o'clock?
Which moment of the day is ten o'clock at night?

grammar.explanation: Preguntamos la edad con «How old are you?». Respondemos con «I’m…» y un número: «I’m six». En esta misión practicamos la pregunta y la respuesta como un intercambio fijo.

items.prompt: Choose the correct answer to “How old are you?”

source.readingText: It is Ella's birthday today. She is seven years old. There is a big cake on the table with seven candles. Her friend Ben has a present and a birthday card. Ben asks, “How old are you, Ella?” Ella smiles and says, “I’m seven!” They sing a birthday song.

source.listeningScript: Ben: Happy birthday, Ella! Ella: Thank you! Ben: How old are you? Ella: I’m eight today. Ben: Here is a card and a present. Ella: Thank you, Ben. Mum: Look at the cake. There are eight candles. Ella: Eight candles! Let’s sing! Ben: Happy birthday!

listeningQuestions.question: How many candles are on the cake?

grammar.explanation: Podemos invitar a alguien a hacer algo con una instrucción sencilla: «Dance, please». El verbo va al principio y usamos «please» para pedirlo con educación. Cuando recibimos algo, respondemos «Thank you».

items.es: El imperativo usa dance en su forma básica.

items.prompt: Someone gives you a gift. What do you say?
items.es: Thank you sirve para dar las gracias.

Balloon significa globo.

source.readingText: It is Mia's birthday party. There are blue and yellow balloons in the room. Music is playing and the children dance. Ben gives Mia a gift. Mia says, “Thank you!” A little girl asks, “Can I have a balloon, please?” Mia gives her a red balloon. Everyone smiles and enjoys the party.

grammar.focus: My favourite… / I like… / I don't like…
grammar.explanation: Usamos «I like…» para decir que algo nos gusta y «I don’t like…» para decir que no nos gusta. También podemos decir «My favourite… is…» para nombrar nuestro favorito. Después ponemos un juguete, una comida o un animal.
grammar.model: My favourite toy is a car. I like animals.
grammar.practice: Clasifica las cosas que te gustan y las que no te gustan y completa una frase modelo.

items.es: Con I usamos like, sin -s.
I don't like expresa un gusto negativo.

items.prompt: Complete: My favourite toy ___ a car.
items.es: Para presentar un favorito usamos My favourite… is…

items.prompt: Choose the sentence about a favourite food.
items.es: El modelo es My favourite + nombre + is…

source.readingText: Hello! My name is Leo. My favourite toy is my red car. I like animals, too. I love dogs and cats. I like apples, but I don't like bananas. My sister likes bananas. Her favourite food is rice. We have different favourite things, but we play together.

readingQuestions.question: Which fruit does Leo not like?

source.listeningScript: Interviewer: What is your favourite thing, Max? Max: My favourite toy is my train. Interviewer: Do you like animals? Max: Yes, I love dogs. Interviewer: What food do you like? Max: I like apples. I don't like bananas. Interviewer: What about your sister? Max: She likes bananas. Her favourite toy is a doll.

listeningQuestions.question: Which food does Max not like?

grammar.focus: Can / can't + verbo en forma básica
grammar.explanation: Usamos «can» para decir que sabemos o podemos hacer algo y «can’t» para decir que no podemos. Después de can o can’t ponemos el verbo en su forma básica: «I can swim» y «I can’t fly».
grammar.model: I can swim. I can’t fly.
grammar.practice: Relaciona cada capacidad con can o can't según la imagen y completa la frase.

items.es: Después de can usamos el verbo base swim.
Can't expresa que no puedes volar.
I can sing expresa capacidad.

items.prompt: Choose the correct verb after can.
items.es: El verbo después de can no lleva -s ni -ing.

source.readingText: This is a school talent day. Anna can sing and dance. Ben can run and jump, but he can't swim. Mia can swim very well. Tom can sing, but he can't fly. The children are happy. They show what they can do at the school show.

readingQuestions.question: Where do the children show their abilities?

source.listeningScript: Listen to the children at the park. Jack can run fast. He can jump, too. Lily can dance and sing. Sam can swim, but he can't fly. A bird can fly. The children look at the bird and smile. “Can you sing?” Jack asks Lily. “Yes, I can!” she says.

listeningQuestions.question: What do the children do when they see the bird?
